request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: Case 9
Age: 6 months 18 days
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment: None

Hospital Course:
Case 9, a 6-month-old boy, was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation and management of his medical conditions. He was diagnosed with epilepsy, infantile spasms, developmental delay, and obesity. During his hospital stay, he underwent genetic testing to identify the underlying cause of his conditions.

Diagnostic Results:
The test results showed a de novo heterozygous missense variant in GABRB3. This variant is associated with epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 43 (EIEE43), a rare autosomal dominant disease. The patient's variant was classified as pathogenic according to the ACMG guidelines. This mutation of the GABRB3 gene is predicted to impact receptor function.

Treatment and Plan:
No treatment was initiated during the patient's hospital stay. The medical team provided the family with a comprehensive report on the results of the diagnostic test and the possible long-term implications of the diagnosis. The patient will continue to receive close medical follow-up and monitoring.

Follow-up:
The patient's family was advised to schedule a follow-up appointment with their primary care physician or a specialist in pediatric neurology to discuss the patient's care plan and the need for any further evaluations or testing.

Overall Impression:
Case 9 is a 6-month-old boy diagnosed with epilepsy, infantile spasms, developmental delay, and obesity. The diagnostic test identified a rare de novo heterozygous missense variant in GABRB3, classified as pathogenic, which is linked to epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile 43 (EIEE43). No treatment was initiated during the hospital stay, and the patient's family has been advised to schedule a follow-up appointment with a specialist in pediatric neurology to discuss the implications of the diagnosis and the patient's care plan.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode centers on infantile spasms with epilepsy, and genetic testing identified the cause as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy 43 (EIEE43).

In ICD-10-AM, infantile spasms are coded to G40.4 (other generalised epilepsy and epileptic syndromes) or G40.8 (other epilepsy). West syndrome and infantile spasms are indexed to G40.4 in ICD-10-AM, and the older WHO version also lists infantile spasms under G40.4. Epileptic encephalopathy is also classified in the G40 block. All of these fall into the three-character category G40, epilepsy.

The alternatives are weaker. A genetic cause could suggest a congenital or chromosomal code in Chapter Q, but a single-gene variant causing epileptic encephalopathy has no Q code, so the neurological manifestation takes priority. Developmental delay (R62 or F88) and obesity (E66) are secondary conditions.

CODE: G40
